source_text: Hoc principali praecepto, quo ne digne quidem malefacere concessum, uniuersa patientiae disciplina succincta est. iam uero percurrentibus nobis causas impatientiae cetera quoque praecepta suis locis respondebunt. si detrimento rei familiaris animus concitatur, omni paene in loco contemnendo saeculo scripturis dominicis commonetur; nec maior ad pecuniae contemptum exhortatio subiacet, quam quod ipse dominus in nullis diuitiis inuenitur. semper pauperes iustificat, diuites praedamnat. ita detriment(or)um patientiae fastidium opulentiae praeministrauit, demonstrans per abiectionem diuitiarum laesuras quoque earum computandas non esse. quod ergo nobis appetere minime opus est, quia nec dominus appetiuit, detruncatum uel etiam ademptum non aegre sustinere debemus. cupiditatem omnium malorum radicem spiritus domini per apostolum pronuntiauit. eam non in concupiscentia alieni tantum constitutam interpretemur: nam et quod nostrum uidetur alienum est; nihil enim nostrum, quoniam dei omnia, cuius ipsi quoque nos. itaque si damno adfecti impatienter senserimus, . de non nostro amissum dolentes adfines cupiditatis deprehendemur.. alienum quaerimus, cum alienum amissum aegre sustinemus. qui damni impatientia concitatur terrena caelestibus anteponendo, de proximo in deum peccat. spiritum enim, quem a domino sumpsit, saecularis rei gratia concutit. libenter igitur terrena amittamus, (ut) caelestia tueamur. totum licet saeculum pereat, dum patientiam lucrifaciam. iam qui minutum sibi aliquid aut furto aut ui aut etiam ignauia non constanter sustinere constituit, nescio an facile uel ex animo ipse rei suae manum inferre possit in causa elemosynae. quis enim ab alio secari omnino non sustinens ipse ferrum in corpore suo ducit? patientia in detrimentis exercitatio est largiendi et communicandi. non piget donare eum, qui non timet perdere. alioquin quomodo duas habens tunicas alteram earum nudo dabit, nisi idem sit, qui auferenti tunicam etiam pallium offerre possit? quomodo amicos de mammona . fabricabimus nobis, si eum in tantum amauerimus, ut amissum non sufferamus? peribimus cum perdito qui hic inuenimus ubi habemus amittere. gentilium est omnibus detrimentis impatientiam adhibere, qui rem pecuniariam fortasse animae anteponant., nam id faciunt, cum lucri cupiditatibus quaestuosa pericula mercimoniorum in mari exercent, cum pecuniae causa etiam in foro nihil f damnationi timendum adgredi dubitant, cum denique ludo et castris sese locant, cum peruia inmemores bestiarum latrocinantur. nos uero secundum diuersitatem, qua cum illis sumus, non animam pro pecunia, sed pecuniam pro anima deponere conuenit, seu sponte in largiendo seu patienter in amittendo.
thought_title: Patience in bearing loss of property
orientation: Tertullian is explaining how the Lord's chief command to love enemies sums up the whole discipline of patience, and now turns to the causes of impatience, beginning with loss of property.
pass_a_gloss: By this chief precept, by which it is not even permitted to do evil to the worthy, the whole discipline of patience is girded up. Now indeed, as we run through the causes of impatience, the remaining precepts also will answer in their own places. If the mind is stirred up by loss of family property, in almost every place it is reminded by the Lord's scriptures to despise the world; nor does a greater exhortation to contempt of money lie at hand, than that the Lord himself is found in no riches. He always justifies the poor, condemns the rich beforehand. Thus the disdain of wealth has supplied beforehand the patience of losses, showing through the casting away of riches that their injuries also are not to be reckoned. Therefore what we need least to desire, because the Lord did not desire it, we ought not to bear with difficulty when it is cut off or even taken away. The Spirit of the Lord through the apostle has declared covetousness to be the root of all evils. Let us not interpret it as established only in desire for another's property: for what seems ours is another's; for nothing is ours, since all things are God's, whose we ourselves also are. Therefore if we feel loss with impatience, grieving over what is lost as not ours, we shall be caught as akin to covetousness. We seek another's property, when we bear with difficulty the loss of another's property. He who is stirred by impatience at loss, by putting earthly things before heavenly things, sins against God in his neighbor. For he shakes the spirit, which he received from the Lord, for the sake of a worldly thing. Therefore let us willingly lose earthly things, so that we may guard heavenly things. Let the whole world perish, provided I gain patience. Now he who has decided not to bear steadily some small loss to himself by theft or force or even negligence, I do not know whether he can easily or from the heart lay his hand on his own property in the cause of almsgiving. For who, not enduring at all to be cut by another, himself draws the knife in his own body? Patience in losses is training for giving and sharing. He does not regret giving, who does not fear losing. Otherwise how will he who has two tunics give one of them to the naked, unless he is the same one who can offer also his cloak to the one taking his tunic? How shall we make friends for ourselves from mammon, if we love it so much that we do not bear its loss? We shall perish with what is lost, we who here find where we have to lose. It belongs to pagans to apply impatience to all losses, who perhaps put money before the soul. For they do this, when with desires for gain they carry out profitable dangers of trade on the sea, when for the sake of money they do not hesitate to undertake in the forum what is to be feared for condemnation, when finally they place themselves in the game and the camp, when forgetful of wild beasts they rob along open roads. But we, according to the difference by which we are with them, ought to lay down not the soul for money, but money for the soul, whether willingly in giving or patiently in losing.

choices.why: Glossary requires 'discipline' for disciplina and 'patience' for patientia; the phrase names the ordered training of Christian life in patience.
Glossary requires 'world' for saeculum, the present world and its goods to be despised.
The vice of desiring property, rendered 'covetousness' to match the biblical root of all evils and the argument about property.
The standard English term for charitable giving to the poor, fitting the context of giving one's tunic.
The biblical term for wealth, kept as 'mammon' to preserve the scriptural allusion to making friends from mammon.
Glossary requires 'pagans' for nationes/gentiles, the non-Christians who put money before the soul.

bible_refs.note: The chief precept to love enemies, bless those who curse, and pray for persecutors, referenced as 'principali praecepto'.
Covetousness as the root of all evils: 'cupiditatem omnium malorum radicem'.
He who has two tunics gives one to the naked: 'duas habens tunicas alteram earum nudo dabit'.
Offering the cloak to the one taking the tunic: 'auferenti tunicam etiam pallium offerre'.
Making friends from mammon: 'amicos de mammona fabricabimus nobis'.

pass_b_english: This chief precept, which does not even allow us to wrong someone who deserves it, girds up the whole discipline of patience. Now as we run through the causes of impatience, the other precepts will answer each in its own place. If the mind is stirred up by loss of property, the Lord's Scriptures remind us in almost every place to despise the world. Nor is there any greater encouragement to despise money than the fact that the Lord himself is found in no riches. He always justifies the poor and condemns the rich beforehand. So the casting away of riches has supplied beforehand a distaste for wealth, showing that when riches are cast aside, the wounds they bring should also be counted as nothing. What we have no need to desire, because the Lord did not desire it, we should not bear with bitterness when it is cut off or even taken away. The Spirit of the Lord declared through the apostle that covetousness is the root of all evils (1 Timothy 6:10). Let us not interpret it as consisting only in desiring what belongs to another. For even what seems to be ours belongs to another. Nothing is ours, since all things are God's, and we ourselves are his. Therefore if we feel impatient when we suffer loss, grieving over the loss of what is not ours, we will be caught as akin to covetousness. We seek what belongs to another when we bear with bitterness the loss of what belongs to another. Whoever is stirred up by impatience at loss, putting earthly things before heavenly things, sins against his neighbor and so against God. For he shakes the spirit he received from the Lord for the sake of a worldly thing. Let us therefore willingly lose earthly things so that we may keep heavenly things. Let the whole world perish, if only I gain patience. Now whoever decides he cannot steadfastly bear the loss of some small thing through theft or force or even negligence, I do not know whether he could easily or from the heart lay his hand on his own property for the sake of almsgiving. For who, not bearing at all to be cut by another, draws the knife himself in his own body? Patience in losses is training for giving and sharing. He does not regret giving who does not fear losing. Otherwise, how will the one who has two tunics give one of them to the naked (Luke 3:11), unless he is the same person who can offer his cloak also to the one taking his tunic (Matthew 5:40)? How will we make friends for ourselves from mammon (Luke 16:9), if we love it so much that we cannot bear to lose it? We will perish with what is lost. Here we find where we have to lose. It belongs to pagans to apply impatience to every loss, since they perhaps put money before the soul. For they do this when they carry out profitable dangers of trade on the sea through desire for gain, when for money's sake they do not hesitate to undertake in the forum what must be feared even at the cost of condemnation, when finally they hire themselves out to the games and the camps, when they rob on open roads, forgetful of the beasts. But we, according to the difference between us and them, should lay down not the soul for money but money for the soul, whether willingly in giving or patiently in losing.
notes: The source text contains two apparent gaps or corruptions: after 'impatienter senserimus,' there is a stray period and a gap before 'de non nostro amissum'; and after 'de mammona' there is a stray period before 'fabricabimus'. The gloss renders the sense as it stands without inventing missing text.

The phrase 'nihil f damnationi timendum' appears to contain a corruption or typographical error ('f' before 'damnationi'); the gloss renders it as 'what is to be feared for condemnation' based on the surrounding sense.

problems.why: 'de proximo' means 'from near at hand' = starting from a near/lesser sin leading to God; not 'from nearby' spatially.
problems.fix: sins against God from what is nearest
problems.ruling: Latin 'de proximo' means 'by the near (thing), i.e., preferring the immediate/earthly', not a spatial 'from nearby' as rendered.

edits.new: sins against God from what is nearest

fixed: Corrected 'from nearby' to 'from what is nearest' for 'de proximo', which means starting from a near or lesser sin and proceeding to sin against God, not spatial proximity.

problems.quote: grieving over what has been lost as if it were not another's
problems.why: Source means 'grieving over the loss of what is not ours'; English reverses the sense to 'as if it were not another's.'
problems.fix: grieving over the loss of what is not ours
problems.ruling: Latin 'de non nostro amissum dolentes' = grieving over loss of what is not ours; English says 'as if it were not another's', reversing sense.
